title: Al-Ardah: The Traditional Sword Dance
summary: How Al-Ardah, the Saudi and Gulf folk performance of poetry, drumming, and synchronized movement with ceremonial swords, celebrates heritage at weddings, National Day, and other occasions.
poll: Old traditions like Al-Ardah are still important today.

versions.title: The Sword Dance
versions.text:
Have you seen men dance with swords? It is a cool dance! It is called Al-Ardah.

People in Saudi Arabia love this dance. It is a very old dance. Long ago, people did it to feel strong and glad.

Men stand in two rows. They face each other. Each man holds a sword up high. They do not fight.

A big drum beats. Boom, boom, boom! The men move with the beat. They sway side to side.

A poet says a poem. A poet makes up words. The other men say words back. It feels like a song.

People do this dance on big days. They do it at weddings. They do it on National Day, too.

In 2015, a big group said this dance is special. It is part of our old ways.

This old dance makes people feel proud. It brings them close together.

In the dance, men stand in two long rows. They face each other, and each man holds a sword up high. No one ever fights with it.

A large drum beats a steady rhythm. The men sway side to side, so their moves match the beat. That is why the dance looks so great.

versions.title: Al-Ardah: A Proud Tradition
versions.text:
Have you ever seen men dance with swords? It is surprisingly striking! For centuries, people in Saudi Arabia have danced this way at special times.

Al-Ardah is a very old dance. Long ago, people danced it at gatherings to feel strong and united.

Today, Al-Ardah is still performed at big events. Men stand in two long rows, facing each other. Each man holds a sword straight up, so the rows look like two walls.

No one ever fights with the sword. It is simply part of the show, like a costume piece.

A large drum sets a steady beat. The dancers sway side to side, and they move together with the beat. This makes the dance look strong and graceful.

Who says the words? A person who recites a poem is called a poet. He chants in a strong voice, and the other men chant words back to him.

People perform Al-Ardah at weddings and family events. It is also done every year on National Day.

In 2015, UNESCO named Al-Ardah part of our shared heritage. Heritage means the old ways a group keeps and passes down.

This proud old dance connects people to their past. It brings whole communities together, and it makes everyone feel proud.

versions.title: Al-Ardah: A Proud Tradition
versions.text:
Have you ever seen men dancing together while holding swords high above their heads? This striking ceremonial performance, known as Al-Ardah, has captivated audiences across Arabia for countless generations.

Communities throughout Saudi Arabia and neighboring Gulf lands have treasured this traditional dance for centuries. According to history, tribes once danced it before or after a long journey, to feel strong and united as a group.

In a typical performance, dancers stand in two long rows, facing each other, almost like two walls of people. Each dancer holds a sword straight up, but no one ever fights with it.

The sword is simply part of the costume and the ceremony, serving as a symbol of honor rather than a weapon. A large drum sets a steady, booming rhythm, and the dancers sway side to side in time with the beat.

Their matching movements make the whole performance look powerful and graceful. A person who recites a poem is called a poet, and he chants in a strong voice, often praising courage or the beauty of the homeland.

The other dancers answer by chanting lines back to him, which feels like a shared song. Today, people perform Al-Ardah at weddings and official state events, and it is also a central tradition of National Day.

In 2015, UNESCO named Al-Ardah part of our shared Intangible Cultural Heritage, an honor shared with other Gulf nations. Heritage means the customs a community keeps and passes down through many generations.

This proud, ancient dance connects performers and audiences to their shared history. It continues to bring whole communities together at some of the happiest times of their lives, young and old alike.

versions.title: Al-Ardah: Heritage in Motion
versions.text:
Anyone who has watched men dancing in unison while holding swords high above their heads understands why Al-Ardah remains a recognizable ceremonial performance on the Arabian Peninsula.

For countless generations, this striking tradition has captivated audiences throughout the region. Communities across Saudi Arabia and neighboring Gulf lands have treasured this dance for centuries.

According to oral history, tribes once performed Al-Ardah before setting out on a journey, or after returning safely. The dance was used to express unity, courage, and belonging.

In a typical performance, dancers stand in two long rows facing each other, almost like two facing walls of people. Each dancer holds a sword straight up, yet the sword is never used for fighting.

It functions purely as part of the costume and the ceremony, a symbol of honor rather than a weapon. A large drum establishes a steady, booming rhythm, and the dancers sway side to side in synchronized movement.

A poet's recitation forms the heart of the performance. He chants lines of poetry in a strong, clear voice, often praising courage or the beauty of the homeland, and the rows of dancers respond by chanting lines back to him.

Today, people perform Al-Ardah at important ceremonies, including weddings and official state events, and it is also a central ceremonial tradition of Saudi National Day.

In 2015, UNESCO, the United Nations agency that protects culture worldwide, listed Al-Ardah as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, an honor shared among several Gulf nations.

Heritage, in this sense, refers to the customs and traditions that a community preserves and passes down through generations. This proud, ancient dance connects performers and audiences alike to their shared history, and it continues to bring entire communities together at some of the happiest and most meaningful moments of their lives.

versions.title: Heritage in Motion: Al-Ardah
versions.text:
Anyone who has personally witnessed men dancing in flawless, disciplined unison while holding ceremonial swords high above their heads readily understands why Al-Ardah remains one of the most recognizable ceremonial performances throughout the entire Arabian Peninsula, a tradition that has genuinely captivated audiences for countless preceding generations.

Communities throughout Saudi Arabia and the wider Gulf region have treasured this traditional dance for many long centuries, and it continues to flourish vigorously today. According to longstanding oral history, tribes once performed Al-Ardah before setting out on a journey, or immediately after returning home safely.

The dance expressed collective unity, courage, and a profoundly shared sense of belonging among all of the people who performed it together. In a typical performance, dancers customarily assemble in two long parallel rows facing one another, closely resembling two facing walls of people standing shoulder to shoulder.

Each dancer holds a sword straight upward, yet the sword is never actually wielded for fighting of any kind; rather, it functions purely as a ceremonial part of the costume, serving as a symbol of honor rather than any instrument of actual combat.

A large drum establishes a steady, resonant, booming rhythm, and the dancers sway side to side in meticulously synchronized movement, timing every sway precisely with each beat, so the entire performance appears powerful, disciplined, and remarkably elegant.

A poet's formal recitation forms the genuine heart of the performance. Standing before the assembled rows, he chants lines of poetry in a strong, resonant voice, frequently praising courage or the enduring beauty of the homeland, while the dancers respond by chanting lines back to him in perfectly timed turn.

Today, people perform Al-Ardah at significant ceremonies, including weddings, family gatherings, and official state events, and it also serves as a genuinely central ceremonial feature of Saudi National Day, performed proudly and enthusiastically every single year.

In 2015, UNESCO, the United Nations agency officially responsible for safeguarding culture worldwide, formally inscribed Al-Ardah on its prestigious list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, a significant honor shared jointly among several Gulf nations.

Heritage, in this particular sense, refers to the customs and traditions that a community deliberately preserves and carefully transmits across many successive generations, so that younger people never forget where they truly come from. This proud, ancient dance powerfully connects performers and audiences alike to their shared history, consistently reaffirming a cultural identity that predates the modern nation itself.

versions.title: Heritage in Motion: Al-Ardah
versions.text:
Anyone who has personally and closely witnessed men dancing in flawless, rigorously disciplined unison while holding ceremonial swords high above their heads readily comprehends why Al-Ardah remains one of the most instantly recognizable ceremonial performances throughout the entire Arabian Peninsula, a venerable tradition that has genuinely captivated audiences for countless preceding generations.

Communities throughout Saudi Arabia and the wider Gulf region have treasured this traditional dance for many long, successive centuries, and it continues to flourish vigorously in the present day. According to longstanding oral history, tribes once performed Al-Ardah before setting out on a perilous journey, or immediately upon returning home safely.

The dance expressed collective unity, courage, and a profoundly shared sense of belonging among all of the many people who performed it together. In a typical performance, dancers customarily assemble in two long parallel rows facing one another, closely resembling two opposing walls of people standing shoulder to shoulder.

Each dancer holds a sword straight upward, yet the sword is never actually wielded for fighting of any genuine kind; rather, it functions purely as a ceremonial element of the costume, serving symbolically as an emblem of honor rather than any practical instrument of combat.

A large drum establishes a steady, resonant, booming rhythm, and the dancers sway side to side in meticulously synchronized, rhythmically precise movement, timing every single sway exactly with each beat, so the entire performance appears powerful, disciplined, and remarkably elegant to onlookers.

A poet's formal recitation constitutes the genuine heart of the performance. Standing before the assembled rows, he chants lines of poetry in a strong, resonant voice, frequently extolling courage or the enduring beauty of the homeland, while the dancers respond by chanting lines back to him in perfectly synchronized turn.

Today, people perform Al-Ardah at significant ceremonies, including weddings, family gatherings, and official state events, and it also serves as a genuinely central ceremonial feature of Saudi National Day, performed proudly and enthusiastically every single year throughout the kingdom.

In 2015, UNESCO, the United Nations agency officially responsible for safeguarding culture worldwide, formally inscribed Al-Ardah on its prestigious list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, a significant and widely celebrated honor shared jointly among several Gulf nations.

Heritage, in this particular sense, refers precisely to the customs and traditions that a community deliberately preserves and painstakingly transmits across many successive generations, so that younger people never forget where they truly come from. This proud, ancient dance powerfully connects performers and audiences alike to their shared history, consistently and powerfully reaffirming a distinctive cultural identity that predates the modern nation-state itself.

keyWords.definition: happening at exactly the same time, matched together
keyWords.example: The swimmers performed a synchronized routine in the pool.

keyWords.definition: relating to a formal event held to mark something important
keyWords.example: The mayor cut a ceremonial ribbon to open the new library.

keyWords.definition: unable to be touched, but still real, such as an idea, custom, or tradition
keyWords.example: Kindness is intangible, but we can still feel its effect.

keyWords.definition: the act of saying something aloud from memory, often in a formal way
keyWords.example: Her recitation of the poem impressed the whole audience.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Al-Ardah is primarily a historical battle reenactment staged for tourists visiting Saudi Arabia each year
UNESCO created Al-Ardah as a brand-new ceremonial tradition in 2015 for the Gulf region
Swords used in Al-Ardah are sharpened before every single performance for safety reasons
Al-Ardah is a ceremonial dance that preserves heritage through synchronized movement and poetic recitation
questions.why: The article centers on Al-Ardah as a ceremonial tradition combining movement and poetry to preserve heritage.

wrong.A: The dance is a performance, not a battle reenactment.
wrong.B: UNESCO recognized the dance; it did not create it.
wrong.C: Sword-sharpening is never mentioned.

questions.stem: According to the article, what does a poet's recitation form?
options: The heart of the performance
A separate event held afterward
A written exam for dancers
A private ceremony with no audience present
questions.why: In the article, the poet's recitation forms the heart of the performance.

wrong.B: The recitation happens during, not after, the performance.
wrong.C: No exam is mentioned.
wrong.D: Audiences are present throughout.

questions.stem: What symbol does the sword represent during the performance, according to the article?
options: A weapon for real combat
A tool used for farming
A symbol of honor
A prize for the fastest dancer in the group
questions.why: In the article, the sword functions as a symbol of honor rather than a weapon.

wrong.A: The article explicitly says it is never used for fighting.
wrong.B: Farming is not mentioned.
wrong.D: No prize is described.

questions.stem: The article describes the dancers' sway as 'synchronized.' Synchronized most nearly means —
options: happening loudly with drums
happening at the same time, matched together
happening only once a year
happening without any rhythm or structure, completely at random each time
questions.why: The article says the dancers' movements are matched so precisely that they look powerful and graceful.

wrong.A: Loudness is not what synchronized describes.
wrong.C: Frequency of the dance is not the meaning.
wrong.D: The dance is tightly matched, not random.

questions.stem: What was the main reason tribes historically performed Al-Ardah before or after a journey?
options: To formally select which poet would be allowed to travel together with them on the journey
To test how sharp their swords were
To decide which tribe was strongest
To express unity, courage, and a sense of belonging
questions.why: In the article, the dance expressed unity, courage, and belonging among the people performing it.

wrong.A: Choosing a poet to travel is not mentioned.
wrong.B: Testing swords is not described.
wrong.C: Comparing tribes' strength is not the stated reason.

questions.stem: Why does the author emphasize that the sword is never used for fighting?
options: To make clear the dance is a ceremonial performance, not combat
To explain how swords are manufactured
To argue that all weapons should be banned
To describe a historical battle in extensive and gruesome detail for dramatic effect
questions.why: Repeating that the sword is only ceremonial frames the dance as performance art, not combat.

wrong.B: Manufacturing is not explained.
wrong.C: The article makes no argument about banning weapons.
wrong.D: No battle is described in the article.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why UNESCO lists Al-Ardah as Intangible Cultural Heritage?
options: Because it exclusively and only ever uses modern electronic instruments imported from abroad
Because it was invented very recently
Because it represents a valuable, long-standing cultural tradition
Because it is performed exclusively indoors
questions.why: UNESCO's recognition reflects the dance's long history and cultural value, as the article describes.

wrong.A: The drum and poetry are traditional, not electronic.
wrong.B: The dance is centuries old, not recent.
wrong.D: Indoor-only performance is never stated.

questions.stem: How is the ceremonial role of the sword in Al-Ardah similar to the role of the poet's recitation?
options: Both are sold as souvenirs after the performance
Both function as meaningful parts of the ceremony rather than practical tools
Both were invented by UNESCO in 2015
Both are performed only by women who have trained in the art for many years
questions.why: Both the sword and the recitation carry symbolic, ceremonial meaning rather than a practical purpose.

wrong.A: Souvenirs are not mentioned.
wrong.C: UNESCO recognized, but did not invent, either element.
wrong.D: The dance is described as performed by men.

HIGH.prompt: The article says Al-Ardah shows how a society can preserve its heritage through ceremonial performance. Do you agree? Support your answer with at least two pieces of evidence from the text.
checklist: I used at least two facts from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.

LOW.stem: What does the big drum do for the dancers?
options: It sets the beat
It says the poem
It holds the swords
It makes the rows
LOW.why: In the text, the men move with the beat of the drum.

wrong.B: The poet says the poem, not the drum.
wrong.C: The men hold the swords themselves.
wrong.D: The men stand in rows by themselves.

LOW.stem: What do the other men do after the poet says a poem?
options: Put down the swords
Beat the big drum
Walk out of the rows
Say words back to him
LOW.why: The text says the other men say words back after the poet.

wrong.A: Each man holds a sword up high.
wrong.B: The text does not say the men beat the drum.
wrong.C: The men stay in their rows.

LOW.stem: Why do people do Al-Ardah at weddings?
options: To fight with swords
To sell old swords
To celebrate with everyone
To teach children to read
LOW.why: People do the dance on big days, and it makes them feel proud and close together.

wrong.A: The men do not fight.
wrong.B: Nothing is sold in the dance.
wrong.D: The text does not say the dance teaches reading.

LOW.stem: In the article, what does the word sway mean?
options: Jump straight up and down
Move side to side slowly
Run around in circles
Stand very still
LOW.why: In the text, the men sway side to side with the beat.

wrong.A: The text says side to side, not up and down.
wrong.C: The men stay in their rows.
wrong.D: Swaying is a movement, so it is not standing still.

MID.stem: What does the poet often chant about?
options: Desert animals
Courage
Trading goods
The sea
MID.why: The text says the poet chants in a strong voice, often about courage.

wrong.A: Desert animals are not mentioned.
wrong.C: Trade is not mentioned.
wrong.D: The sea is not mentioned.

MID.stem: In the article, what does the word graceful mean?
options: Loud and wild
Slow and sad
Fast and rough
Smooth and beautiful
MID.why: The dancers sway together with the beat, which looks strong and graceful, so graceful means smooth and beautiful.

wrong.A: Swaying together is calm, not wild.
wrong.B: The dance is proud, not sad.
wrong.C: The text describes steady, smooth movement.

MID.stem: What makes the dance look strong and graceful?
options: Swaying with the drum
Fighting with swords
Running between the rows
Singing without a poet
MID.why: In the text, the dancers sway side to side together with the beat, which makes the dance look strong and graceful.

wrong.B: The text says no one ever fights with a sword.
wrong.C: The men stand in rows and do not run between them.
wrong.D: The poet is part of the dance.

MID.stem: Why does the author begin with a question?
options: To teach how to dance
To warn about sword danger
To get readers curious
To ask for a vote
MID.why: The opening question makes readers picture men dancing with swords and want to read more.

wrong.A: The article does not teach dance steps.
wrong.B: The swords are never used for fighting.
wrong.D: The article does not ask for a vote.

HIGH.stem: According to the article, with whom is the UNESCO honor shared?
options: With every nation on Earth
Only within one Saudi town
With a single desert tribe
Among several Gulf nations
HIGH.why: The article says the honor is shared among several Gulf nations.

wrong.A: In the article, several Gulf nations, not every nation.
wrong.B: The honor is shared by more than one town.
wrong.C: The article does not name a single tribe.

HIGH.stem: What does the word heritage mean as the article explains it?
options: Money left to a family member
Customs passed down over time
Rules written by a government
Buildings made of stone
HIGH.why: In the article, heritage refers to the customs and traditions a community preserves and passes down.

wrong.A: The article does not mean money.
wrong.C: Heritage is about customs, not government rules.
wrong.D: Buildings are not mentioned.

HIGH.stem: What effect does the drum's steady rhythm have on the dancers?
options: They run toward the audience
They put down their swords
They sway together in time
They begin chanting poetry alone
HIGH.why: The article says a booming drum sets a steady rhythm and the dancers sway side to side in synchronized movement.

wrong.A: The dancers stay in their rows.
wrong.B: Each dancer keeps the sword held up.
wrong.D: The poet chants, and the rows answer him.

HIGH.stem: Why does the article end by describing happy moments?
options: To show why it still matters
To explain how swords are made
To list the dates of weddings
To say the dance is now rare
HIGH.why: The ending says the dance connects people to their history and brings communities together at meaningful moments.

wrong.B: Making swords is not explained.
wrong.C: No wedding dates are listed.
wrong.D: The dance still brings communities together.
